title: Landlord-Tenant Law in Depth
originality: All items original to LicensePath. Modeled on the DRE exam blueprint and style only; no actual exam items reproduced.

options: Can be waived if both parties agree in writing
Cannot be waived by the lease
Applies only in the first year of tenancy
rationales: It cannot be waived even by written agreement.
Correct. It is non-waivable as a matter of public policy.
It applies to residential leases, not commercial.
It applies throughout the tenancy, not only the first year.

questions.stem: The implied warranty of habitability requires that a unit be:
options: Fit for human habitation and free of health/safety hazards
rationales: Luxury finishes are not required.
Correct. Basic livability and safety are the standard.
Rent control status is unrelated.
Ownership structure is unrelated to habitability.

questions.stem: California's Tenant Protection Act (AB 1482) generally imposes:
options: A statewide rent cap and just-cause eviction requirement for most covered tenancies
A requirement that all units be rent-controlled locally
rationales: It does impose limits for covered tenancies.
Correct. It caps annual rent increases and requires just cause for eviction in most covered cases.
It does not ban all evictions; it requires just cause.
Local rent control is separate and additional, not required by AB 1482 itself.

questions.stem: Just cause for eviction generally falls into which two categories?
rationales: This is not the standard categorization.
Correct. Just cause is generally categorized as at-fault or no-fault.
This is not the standard categorization used.
This is not the standard categorization used.

questions.stem: An owner moving into the unit is generally an example of:
rationales: The tenant is not at fault in this scenario.
Correct. Owner move-in is a no-fault just cause category, often triggering relocation assistance.
This is not retaliation against the tenant.
This is not about habitability failure.

questions.stem: Self-help eviction, such as changing locks or shutting off utilities without a court judgment, is:
options: Legal if the tenant is clearly behind on rent
Illegal regardless of how clearly the tenant is in default
rationales: Clear tenant default does not legalize self-help eviction.
Correct. Self-help eviction is illegal regardless of the merits of the underlying claim.
This applies broadly, not only to commercial tenants in a way that changes the rule here.
Notice alone does not make self-help eviction legal.

questions.stem: The court process required to lawfully remove a tenant is called:
rationales: Quiet title concerns ownership disputes, not eviction.
Correct. Unlawful detainer is the required court process for eviction.
Probate concerns estates, not eviction.
Workers' compensation is unrelated.

questions.stem: After a landlord wins an unlawful detainer judgment, physical removal of the tenant may be carried out by:
options: The sheriff under a writ of possession
rationales: Landlords may not personally remove tenants.
Property managers also may not personally remove tenants.
Correct. Only the sheriff, under a writ of possession, may carry out physical removal.
A locksmith alone does not have authority to remove a tenant.

questions.stem: Constructive eviction requires that the tenant:
options: Stay in the unit and stop paying rent
Give notice, allow a reasonable cure period, and actually vacate
Sue for damages without moving out
rationales: Staying and withholding rent is a weaker legal position than constructive eviction requires.
Correct. Notice, a cure opportunity, and actual vacatur are generally required.
A damages suit without vacating does not establish constructive eviction.
Bankruptcy is unrelated to this doctrine.

questions.stem: A tenant who reports a serious mold problem, waits a reasonable time for repair despite repeated requests, then vacates after continued inaction has a strong claim of:
rationales: Retaliation is not the fact pattern here.
Correct. Unremedied serious habitability failure plus proper notice and vacatur is constructive eviction.
Self-help eviction describes illegal landlord lockout conduct, not this scenario.
Adverse possession is unrelated to this scenario.

questions.stem: A landlord raises rent shortly after a tenant files a code enforcement complaint about habitability. This can trigger:
options: A rebuttable presumption of retaliatory eviction
Immediate unlawful detainer against the landlord
rationales: The complaint is not automatically dismissed by this conduct.
Correct. California law creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation when adverse action follows protected activity within a statutory window.
Unlawful detainer applies to removing tenants, not this scenario.
There can be real legal consequence for the landlord.

questions.stem: Normal wear and tear, such as faded paint or worn carpet from ordinary use, is:
options: Not chargeable against the security deposit
Chargeable only if the tenant stayed over a year
rationales: It cannot be charged to the tenant.
Correct. Normal wear and tear is an ownership cost, not tenant damage.
This distinction applies broadly, not only commercial leases.
Tenancy length does not change this rule.

questions.stem: When deducting from a security deposit, a landlord must generally:
options: Provide an itemized statement and, for larger deductions, documentation
Keep the entire deposit regardless of condition
Wait indefinitely to return the balance
rationales: An explanation is required.
Correct. Itemization and documentation for larger deductions are required, with the balance returned within a statutory period.
The landlord may not simply keep the full deposit without basis.
There is a statutory time limit to return the balance.

questions.stem: Repair-and-deduct as a tenant remedy generally:
options: Allows unlimited repairs deducted at any time
Has statutory dollar and frequency limits with procedural notice requirements
Requires no prior notice to the landlord
Is available only to commercial tenants
rationales: It is not unlimited; statutory limits apply.
Correct. Statutory limits and required notice/procedure apply before a tenant may use this remedy.
Prior notice is generally required.
It is a residential tenant remedy in this context.

questions.stem: Rent withholding as a habitability remedy:
options: Carries no risk to the tenant
Carries real risk of eviction if the justification is later found insufficient
Is always the safest tenant option
rationales: It carries real legal risk.
Correct. If a court finds the withholding unjustified, the tenant risks an eviction action.
It is a genuinely risky remedy, not the safest option by default.
Careful documentation is essential to support the claim.

questions.stem: A landlord frustrated with the unlawful detainer timeline changes the locks while the tenant is at work. Even if the tenant genuinely owes back rent, the landlord:
options: Has acted lawfully because the tenant was in default
Has committed an independently illegal act exposing them to statutory damages
Has no liability since it saved court costs
Must only pay a small administrative fine
rationales: Tenant default does not excuse self-help eviction.
Correct. Self-help eviction is illegal on its own terms, regardless of the underlying claim's merit.
Liability is real and can be significant, not avoided by cost savings.
The exposure is a real damages claim, not merely a small fine.

questions.stem: A licensee involved in property management who encounters a genuine just-cause compliance question should:
options: Recognize the issue, document it, and refer to an attorney or specialized expertise
Ignore it since it is the owner's problem
Tell the tenant the eviction is definitely valid
rationales: Guessing on a legal compliance question risks real harm.
Correct. Recognize, document, and refer is the consistent professional standard.
Property managers have real duties here; it is not simply the owner's problem alone.
Definitively confirming validity is a legal determination outside license scope.

questions.stem: Exemptions from all or part of California's statewide rent cap and just-cause framework can include:
options: Certain single-family homes and condos with proper notice, and some newer construction
rationales: Exemptions do exist for certain property types.
Correct. Certain single-family/condo properties with proper notice and newer construction can be exempt, subject to specific requirements.
Ownership structure alone does not determine exemption.
The framework is a California state law; this option is not the relevant exemption category.
